agent_notes: The famous crux: 'to the wicked, in the midst of my heart'. The Masoretic text has לִבִּי 'my heart', which makes no easy sense of a sin speaking inside the psalmist; LXX and Syriac read 'his heart' (לבו). I kept the Hebrew 'my heart' in the literal layer, as the packet's pointing and the medieval commentators (Rashi, Radak, Malbim) all do, reading it as the psalmist hearing the voice of Transgression within himself and then reporting it. KJV, ASV and Webster follow the Hebrew; BBE silently moves to 'his heart'. The dramatic layer keeps 'my heart' too.
Last clause: STEPBible glosses אֱלֹהִים as deity.yhwh. Here it is the generic 'God' of 'fear of God'; I glossed it plainly as 'God' and kept it 'God', not YHWH, in the literal layer.

The verse is hard and the five English versions split: KJV/Webster 'until his iniquity be found to be hateful', ASV/BBE 'that his iniquity will not be found out and be hated', YLT a bare literal. I kept the Hebrew order and gave the readings in the commentary, each to its own source: Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David (God finds his iniquity and hates it); Radak and Meiri (he searches out the evil deed until he finds it, and hates the good way); the ASV reading is not in the packet's commentaries. The dramatic layer follows the self-soothing sense, the one closest to ASV/BBE. 'He has made smooth' departs from STEPBible only in adding the idiom; my reading, with BDB behind it.
